la:verb:dimitto.gloss: to send away, send forth, send off, dismiss, let go
senses: to send away, send forth, send off, dismiss, let go
to renounce, give up, abandon, forego, forsake
la:verb:dimitto.html:
dī-mitto, mīsi, missum, 3, v. a.
With particular reference to the prep., to send different ways, to send apart, i. e.,

To send out or forth in different directions, to send about (class.).

With acc.: Naevius pueros circum amicos dimittit,: consules designatos circum provincias,: litteras circum municipia,; cf.: litteras circa praefectos,: litteras per omnes provincias,; with which cf.: nuntios per agros,: librum per totam Italiam,: edicta per provincias,: certos per litora, et saep.: nuntios tota civitate Aeduorum,: nuntios in omnes partes,; 4, 34, 5; cf. ; and poet.: aciem (i. e. oculos) in omnes partes,: praefectos in finitimas civitates,; cf.: Manlium Faesulas, et saep.: nuntios ad Centrones, etc.,; so with ad, ; al.: legatos quoquoversus,; ; : dimissos equites pabulandi causa,; cf. equitatum,: omnem ab se equitatum, § 1.—Trop.: animum ignotas in artes,, directs, applies (al. demittit).—
Without object acc.: dimisit circum omnes propinquas regiones,: per provincias,: ad amicos, Fragm. § 22; cf.: in omnes partis,.—
To separate a multitude, to break up, dissolve; and subjectively, to dismiss (from one's self), to discharge, disband: senatu dimisso,: senatum,: concilium,; ; ; ; et saep.; cf. conventum,: exercitum (a standing military t. t.; cf. ), ; et saep.: plures manus (with diducere, and opp. continere manipulos ad signa),: delectum,: convivium,to break up,; et saep.
With particular reference to the verb, to send away either an individual or a body; to let go, discharge, dismiss, release.
Lit.: aliquem ab se et amandare in ultimas terras,; so, aliquem ab se,; : discedentem aliquem non sine magno dolore,fin.: aliquos aequos placatosque,; so, aliquem incolumem,; : ex custodia,: e carcere,: impunitum,: saucium ac fugatum,: neminem nisi victum, et saep.; cf.: aliquem ludos pessumos, i. e. pessime ludificatum,: uxorem,i. e. to put her away, repudiate her,: Cossutia dimissa, quae desponsata fuerat, etc.,: sponsam intactam,: cf. also: aliquam e matrimonio,; v. also under no. B.: creditorem,i. e. to pay him,, 72: debitorem,i. e. to forgive him the debt,: equos, in order to fight on foot,; ; but also in order to flee,: hostem ex manibus,; 3, 49, 2; cf. also: Demosthenem (i. e. his orations) e manibus,to put out of one's hands, to lay down,; cf.: istos sine ulla contumelia dimittamus,: milites, in oppidum,: a turpissima suspicione,to free, relieve,.—Absol.: dimittam, ut te velle video,; ; —
Transf., of inanimate objects: eum locum, quem ceperant,to abandon, desert,: Italiam,: ripas,: complura oppida,: provinciam,: captam Trojam, et saep.: fortunas morte,; cf. patrimonium,: speratam praedam ex manibus,: signa ex metu,; cf. arma,; et saep.— Esp.: dimissis manibus, with hands relaxed, i. e. in all haste: ibi odos dimissis manibus in caelum volat,; cf.: dimissis pedibus, v. 54: dimissis manibus fugere domum,.—
Trop., to renounce, give up, abandon, forego, forsake: ista philosophia, quae nunc prope dimissa revocatur,, 4, 11: rem saepius frustra tentatam,: exploratam victoriam,: oppugnationem,; : occasionem rei bene gerendae,; cf. ; : rei gerendae facultatem,; 3, 97, 1: omnem rei frumentariae spem,: condiciones pacis,: principatum,: tempus,fin.; : suum jus (opp. retinere),: vim suam,: libertatem; : amicitias,: commemorationem nominis nostri,: quaestionem,: curam,; : praeterita, instantia, futura pari oblivione,: matrimonia,: fugam,: coeptum iter,: cursus, et saep.: tantam fortunam ex manibus,: studium et iracundiam suam rei publicae dimittere, i. q. condonare,to sacrifice to the good of the state,; cf.: tributa alicui,i. e. to remit,: laudibus nomen alicujus in longum aevum,to transmit,: dimissum quod nescitur, non amittitur,is foregone, not lost, (Rib.).

la:adj:dimidius.html:
dī-mĭdĭus, a, um, adj.
medius
,
half (for the diff. between it and dimidiatus, v. dimidio).
As an adj., until the Aug. per. only in connection with pars, e. g.: dimidiam partem nationum subegit,; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; (twice); ; ; ; ; et saep.—
Since the Aug. per., esp. in poets, also with other substantives, instead of dimidiatus (v. dimidio), divided into two equal parts, halved: mullus (opp. lupus totus),: crus,: vultus,: Memnone,: forma circuli,: clepsydrae,: labro basia dare,i. e. slightly, and 22; so of busts: Priapus,; cf. Cicero's pun on the half-length likeness of his brother Quintus: frater meus dimidius major est quam totus, in (the word dimidius, for dimidiatus, belongs prob. to Macr. himself).—
Trop., so of persons of mixed descent: dimidius patrum, dimidius plebis,half patrician and half plebeian,. —Hence, subst.
dīmidium, ii, n., the half (very freq. in all periods and kinds of writing): horae, Lucil. ap. ; so with gen., ; ; et saep.; absol., ; ; ; et saep.; abl. dimidio, with comparatives: dimidio minus opinor,less by half,; ; ; ; ; et saep.—
Like a comp. with quam: vix dimidium militum quam quod acceperat successori tradidit,; .—Prov.: dimidium facti, qui coepit, habet,well begun is half done,; cf. .—
Rarely dī-midia, ae, f. (sc. pars), the half: verbenaca decocta in aqua ad dimidias,.

la:verb:dimidio.html:
dīmĭdĭo, no
perf., ātum, 1, v. a.
dimidius
, to divide into two equal parts, to halve (as a finite verb, very rare): quid dimidias Christum?.— Trop.: viri dolosi non dimidiabunt dies suos,i. e. shall not live half the life of men,; cf. also, id. Job, 21, 21; but freq. and class. in the perf. part.dīmĭ-dĭātus, halved, half (acc. to Varr. ap. , applied to a whole, which is divided into halves; whereas dimidius is applied to a half; or, as Gellius rightly explains it, dimidiatum nisi ipsum, quod divisum est, dici haud convenit; dimidium vero est, non quod ipsum dimidiatum est, sed quae ex dimidiato pars altera est; cf. however, dimidius, I.): homines dimidiati, Cato ap. Gell. l. l.; cf. ; and comic.: procellunt sese in mensam dimidiati (with half the body), dum appetunt, ; cf. also, transf.: dies quidem jam ad umbilicum est dimidiatus mortuus,: luna, Cato ap. ; cf. mensis,; : vas vini, Enn. ap. Gell. l. l.: porcus, Lucil. ib.; cf. : solea, Lucil. ap. Gell. l. l.: librum, fabulam legi, Varr. ib.; cf.: exesis posterioribus partibus versiculorum, dimidiatis fere,; so the comic verse respecting Terence: tu quoque, tu in summis, o dimidiate Menander, etc., Caes. ap. Suet. Vita Ter. fin.

la:noun:dimicatio.html:
dīmĭcātĭo, ōnis, f.
dimico
,
a fight, combat, furious encounter (cf.: pugna, proelium, certamen, contentio, acies; freq. and good prose).
Lit., ; ; ; fin.; ; ; ; et saep.—In plur., ; .—
With gen.: proelii,: universae rei,a pitched battle, general engagement,; for which, universa,. —
Transf. beyond the milit. sphere, a combating, struggling; a contest: non modo contentione, sed etiam dimicatione elaborandum,: talis in remp. nostram labor, assiduitas, dimicatio,; ; ; —
With gen.: vitae,i. e. a perilous contest,: capitis,; cf.: capitis, famae, fortunarumque omnium,: fortunae (c. c. discrimen),.

la:verb:dimico.html:
dī-mĭco, āvi (e. g. dimicavere, ;
dimicaverant,; dimicassent,; dimicuisse,; ), ātum, 1, v. n., lit., to brandish one's weapons against the enemy, i. e. to fight, struggle, contend (freq. and class.).
Lit.: manum conserere atque armis dimicare,: armis cum aliquo,: ferro pro patria,: acie cum aliquo,; for which: in acie,: proelio,; 6, 31, 1 al.: equitatu,: adversus aliquem,: pro legibus, pro libertate, pro patria, et saep.: tuto dimicare,; so absol., ; 3, 17 fin. et saep.—Pass. impers.: ancipiti proelio dimicatur,; so, proelio,; 3, 72, 3 al.; and without proelio,; ; ; cf.: in mortem dimicabatur,—In partic. of gladiatorial combats, ; ; ; ; —
With an abstr. subject: leonum feritas inter se non dimicat, prooem. § 5.
Transf. beyond the milit. sphere, to struggle, to strive, to contend: omni ratione erit dimicandum, ut, etc., : dimicantes competitores,: de sua potentia periculo civitatis,; esp. with the accessory idea of risk, hazard: reos, de capite, de fama, de civitate, de fortunis, de liberis dimicantes (for which, shortly before: qui auderent se et salutem suam in discrimen offerre), : de honore et gloria (for which, shortly before: de vita, de gloria in discrimen vocantur), : de vita gloriae causa,; cf.: de vita,fin.; : de omnibus fortunis reip., Pompei. ap. D.: de fama,: de liberis,; and: de repulsa,i. e. at the risk of one,; cf. also without de: ut in singulas horas capite dimices tuo, (in , the reading is dubious, v. Madv. ad h. l.).—
In Tertullian, borrowed from the lang. of gladiators (v. supra, no. I.): ad hanc jam lineam dimicabit nostra congressio,; .

la:verb:dimoveo.gloss: to move, move aside, or put asunder; part, separate, divide, dislodge, cleave; remove, take away
senses: to move, move aside, or put asunder; part, separate, divide, dislodge, cleave; remove, take away
la:verb:dimoveo.html:
dī-mŏvĕo, ōvi, ōtum (DISMOTUM,
v.infra), 2, v. a. (in MSS. and edd. often confounded with demoveo, q. v.; not freq. before the Aug. per.; not in Caes. and Quint.; perh. not in Cic., where demovere appears everywhere to be the better reading).
To move asunder, to part, put asunder, separate, divide: terram aratro,; cf.: glebas aratro,: aera (c. c. dispellere umbras),; cf. auras,: cinerem foco,: undas,; ; cf. aquas,; : rubum,.—Poet.: ubi sol radiis terram dimovit abortus (preceded by: ubi roriferis terram nox obruit umbris),cleaves the earth, lays it open,.—
Transf.
Of a multitude of persons or things, to separate from each other, to scatter, disperse, drive away, dismiss: humentem umbram polo,; ; cf.: gelidam umbram caelo,: obstantes propinquos,: turbam,; ; ; cf.: dimotis omnibus,; cf.: VTEI EA BACANALIA SEI QVA SVNT ... DISMOTA SIENT, i. e. be dissolved, abolished, S. C. de Bacchan. fin.—
To separate from something, to remove.
Lit.: quos (equites) spes societatis a plebe dimoverat,; : dimovit perfregitque custodias Poena,: parietes (al. demotis),: plagulas (lecticae),—
Trop.: gaudentem patrios findere sarculo Numquam dimoveas, ut, etc., thou canst never entice away, in order to, etc., (al. demo-).—
To move to and fro, to put in motion (cf. dimitto, no. I.—so perh. only in Celsus): superiores partes,: manus,: se inambulatione levi,

senses: which is to be sent away or dismissed

la:noun:dimensio.html:
dīmensĭo, ōnis, f.
dimetior
,
a measuring.
Prop.: quadrati,.—
Transf., the axis of the earth, Hygin. Astr. 1, 3.—
Extent, dimensions, in gen., ; —So plur. .—
Trop.: vocum,: versuum,; cf. and 85.

la:verb:dimetior.html:
dī-mētĭor, mensus, 4,
v. dep. a., to measure any thing, to measure out (v. demetior init.—rare but class.): studium dimetiendi caeli atque terrae,: dimetiri et dinumerare syllabas,: campum ad certamen,: mundum,; cf. .—Hence, part. as subst.: dīmētĭens, entis, f., the diameter (διάμετρος), !*? In pass. signif.: columnae altitudo dimetiatur in partes duodecim,; ; : mirari se sollertiam ejus, a quo essent illa dimensa atque descripta,; so in the part., ; ; ; ; ; .—Cf. in fut. pass. part.: non cum vitae tempore esse dimetiendam commemorationem nominis nostri, Halm (Baiter, dimittendam).

la:verb:diminuo.gloss: to break into small pieces; to shatter
senses: to break into small pieces; to shatter
la:verb:diminuo.html:
dī-mĭnŭo (or dimmĭnuo), ĕre,
v. a., to break into small pieces, to dash to pieces, to break (v. deminuo—rare; perh. only ante-class.): qui ego illi speculo dimminuam caput,; cf.: caput homini,: caput tuum,: cerebrum tibi,; .—
To violate, outrage, destroy by outrage: veritates,: de verbis libri, (perh. deminuerit is a better reading).

dĭmĕter (-trus), a, um, adj., = δίμετρος,

la:noun:dimissio.html:
dīmissĭo, ōnis, f.
dimitto
.
A sending in different directions, a sending out, sending forth (very rare): dimissiones libertorum ad faenerandas provincias,: sanguinis,i. e. blood-letting,in lemm.—*
A dismissing, discharging: propugnatorum atque remigum,.—
The remission (of pain, fever, etc.; opp. accessio),;
